title: ASC 730 Directive
description: The ASC 730 Directive is an IRS LB&I safe harbor letting large taxpayers use adjusted ASC 730 R&D expense as evidence of qualified research expenses.
summary: The ASC 730 Directive is an IRS LB&I administrative safe harbor that lets large corporate taxpayers (assets of $10 million or more) filing U.S. GAAP Certified Audited Financial Statements use mechanically adjusted ASC 730 R&D expense as sufficient evidence of Qualified Research Expenses for the federal research credit under IRC Section 41, without project-by-project technical substantiation.

body.text: The ASC 730 Directive is an IRS LB&I administrative safe harbor that lets large corporate taxpayers (assets of $10 million or more) filing U.S. GAAP Certified Audited Financial Statements use mechanically adjusted ASC 730 R&D expense as sufficient evidence of Qualified Research Expenses for the federal research credit under IRC Section 41, without project-by-project technical substantiation.

Corporate taxpayers claiming the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 navigate a structurally bifurcated regulatory regime in which financial accounting standards under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) diverge sharply from federal income tax law. To mitigate the administrative friction of project-by-project technical audits for large corporate filers, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Large Business and International (LB&I) division issued the ASC 730 Directive—originally signed on September 11, 2017, under Control Number LB&I-04-0917-005 and revised on September 10, 2020, under Control Number LB&I-04-0820-0016 (codified in Internal Revenue Manual [IRM] 4.30.2.11.3 and IRM 4.30.2.11.4, and detailed in LB&I Practice Unit DCN COR-P-032). The Directive establishes an administrative evidentiary safe harbor under which LB&I examiners accept a mechanically adjusted U.S. GAAP financial statement research and development figure—termed Adjusted ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D (ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D)—as sufficient substantiation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC Section 41 without requiring bottom-up engineering proof of the statutory four-part qualification test.

Eligibility for this administrative safe harbor is strictly limited to LB&I taxpayers—corporate entities holding assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000—that prepare Certified Audited Financial Statements (CAFS) in accordance with U.S. GAAP, separately disclose currently expensed Financial Statement R&D on the income statement or in the financial statement notes, and (under the 2020 Revised Directive) utilize those exact same U.S. GAAP financial statements to reconcile book income to federal tax income on Schedule M-3 on an original timely filed return. While the Directive substantially compresses audit timelines and documentation burdens for baseline QRE claims, its operational utility has been tested by two major regulatory developments: the mandatory capitalization and amortization of Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures enacted under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) amendments to IRC Section 174 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 (and subsequently modified for domestic expenditures paid or incurred in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, by the enactment of IRC Section 174A under Public Law 119-21, the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act [OBBBA]), and the structural overhaul of IRS Form 6765 introducing Section G (Business Component Information).
Regulatory Bifurcation of Research and Development Expenditures
Divergence Between Financial Accounting and Federal Tax Frameworks

Financial accounting and federal income taxation in the United States govern research and development (R&D) expenditures through structurally distinct regulatory frameworks, creating substantial compliance friction for corporate taxpayers. Under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), financial reporting prioritizes accounting conservatism by requiring the immediate expensing of R&D outlays in the period incurred, whereas the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) bifurcates research expenditures into incremental credit-eligible outlays under IRC Section 41 and research or experimental (R&E) expenditures governed by the capitalization and deduction regimes of IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 174A.

To bridge the administrative divide between financial statement presentation and tax credit substantiation, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Large Business and International (LB&I) division issued its administrative guidance titled Guidance for Allowance of the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under I.R.C. § 41 for Taxpayers that Expense Research and Development Costs on their Financial Statements pursuant to ASC 730. Originally issued on September 11, 2017 (LB&I Control No. LB&I-04-0917-005, impacting IRM 4.51.2 and applicable to tax years ending prior to July 31, 2020) and formally revised on September 10, 2020 (LB&I Control No. LB&I-04-0820-0016, applicable to original timely filed returns for tax periods ending on or after July 31, 2020), the ASC 730 Directive establishes an administrative framework that leverages the consistency and independent third-party verification of audited U.S. GAAP financial reporting to streamline the rigorous substantiation otherwise required to claim Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC Section 41. Within IRS examination operations, participation in the Directive is codified under IRM 4.30.2.11.3 and IRM 4.30.2.11.4 and monitored using LB&I Project Code 1511 and Tracking Code 6750. In addition, Section 4.03 of Revenue Procedure 2024-30 cross-references the Directive's framework under the automatic accounting method change procedures of Revenue Procedure 2015-13, and the IRS Pre-Filing Agreement (PFA) program specifically asks corporate applicants to state whether they anticipate following LB&I-04-0820-0016.

Eligibility for the ASC 730 Directive is bounded by entity size, accounting methodology, and financial reporting rigor. Only LB&I taxpayers—defined as corporate entities possessing assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000 (including qualifying taxpayers participating in the Compliance Assurance Process [CAP])—may apply the Directive; Small Business/Self-Employed (SB/SE) taxpayers and non-LB&I entities are excluded even if they prepare audited financial statements. Furthermore, a qualifying taxpayer must prepare its financial statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP—taxpayers reporting under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are ineligible—and must explicitly disclose the amount of currently expensed ASC 730 R&D costs either as a standalone line item on the income statement or as a separately stated disclosure in the notes to its Certified Audited Financial Statements (CAFS). Merely disclosing R&D tax credits as deferred income tax assets in a tax footnote does not satisfy this requirement. Under the 2020 Revised Directive (LB&I-04-0820-0016), an eligible taxpayer must also use the exact same U.S. GAAP CAFS to reconcile book income to federal tax income on Schedule M-3 (checking Part I, Line 4(b) to confirm U.S. GAAP was used) and must elect to follow the Directive on an original timely filed federal income tax return (including extensions). Taxpayers may choose whether to follow the Directive on a year-by-year basis; while a taxpayer cannot file an amended return to adopt the Directive if it did not follow the Directive on its original return, a taxpayer that followed the Directive on an original return may file an amended return under Notice 2008-39 guidelines to correct a calculation error in its ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D amount, subject to IRS examination risk assessment.

Under Appendix E of the Directive, a financial statement qualifies as a Certified Audited Financial Statement only if it is accompanied by the report of an independent Certified Public Accountant (as defined under American Institute of Certified Public Accountants [AICPA] Professional Standards, Code of Professional Conduct, Rule 101 and its interpretations and rulings) attesting that the financial statement is either certified to be fairly presented via an unqualified ("clean") opinion or subject to a qualified opinion that the statement is fairly presented subject to a specified concern. Because falsifying ASC 730 disclosures on audited financial statements can equate to fraud and independent CPAs will not risk their professional certification to misstate GAAP R&D expenses, this independent attestation provides the external verification necessary for the IRS to rely upon the financial accounting baseline as a starting point for tax adjustments.
Authoritative GAAP Baseline Under FASB ASC 730

Codified by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 730 (Research and Development) serves as the authoritative U.S. GAAP standard governing R&D expenditures for nongovernmental entities. Because research and development activities carry inherent uncertainty regarding future economic benefits until technological and commercial viability is confirmed, ASC 730 mandates that R&D costs generally be charged to expense immediately as incurred.

As explicitly defined in Appendix E of the Directive, the regulatory architecture of ASC 730 structures financial accounting and reporting around four core elements: (1) the identification of those activities that shall be identified as research and development for financial accounting and reporting purposes; (2) the delineation of the specific elements of costs that shall be identified with research and development activities; (3) the prescription of the accounting treatment requiring immediate expensing of research and development costs; and (4) the mandate of explicit financial statement disclosures related to research and development costs. Within the FASB codification hierarchy, ASC 730-10 (Overall) is organized into subtopics covering Status (00), Overview and Background (05), Objectives (10), Scope and Scope Exceptions (15), Glossary (20), Recognition (25), Disclosure (50), Implementation Guidance and Illustrations (55), Relationships (60), and XBRL Elements (75).

The functional scope of qualifying activities under ASC 730 is broad, encompassing laboratory research aimed at discovering new knowledge, searching for applications of new research findings, conceptual formulation and design of possible product or process alternatives, preproduction prototyping and model construction, and the modification or testing of products and processes. Conversely, ASC 730-10-15-4 and ASC 730-10-55-2 identify routine or commercial transactions and activities typically excluded from ASC 730 R&D, such as engineering services performed during early phases of commercial production involving routine, ongoing efforts to improve an existing product, or quality control during commercial production.

Crucially, ASC 730-10-50-1 mandates that disclosure shall be made in the financial statements of the total R&D costs charged to expense in each period for which an income statement is presented, and specifies that such disclosure shall include R&D costs incurred for a computer software product to be sold, leased, or otherwise marketed. Under U.S. GAAP and the IRS Directive FAQs, software development costs are bifurcated across distinct accounting standards that directly govern what may remain in the ASC 730 Directive baseline:

items: Externally Marketed Software (ASC 985-20): For software developed to be sold, leased, or otherwise marketed—where customers have the contractual right and ability to take possession of the software and run it on their own or an unrelated third party's hardware, or where software is embedded in a physical product or process such as semiconductor chips—ASC 985-20-25-1 and 25-2 dictate that specified costs incurred up to the point of establishing technological feasibility (when all planning, designing, coding, and testing activities necessary to establish that the product can be produced to meet its design specifications, including functions, features, and technical performance requirements, are completed) are booked as ASC 730 R&D costs. Once technological feasibility is established, subsequent activities and costs are no longer ASC 730 activities and costs.

Internal-Use Software (ASC 350-40) and Hosting/Cloud Arrangements (ASC 985-20-15-5 through 15-7): Costs associated with software developed or modified solely to meet a taxpayer's internal needs under ASC 350-40, as well as software provided through cloud computing or Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) hosting arrangements (governed by ASC 985-20-15-5 through 15-7 and ASC 350-40-20 / 65-3) where the end user accesses the software online on an as-needed basis without taking contractual possession, are generally excluded from ASC 730 R&D costs. Under the 2020 Revised Directive, any non-ASC 730 cloud/SaaS or internal-use software development costs reported in the financial statement R&D line item must be mechanically removed in Step 2 (Line 3a) of Appendix C, as ASC 730 contains no equivalent to the tax law's three-part High Threshold of Innovation test for internal-use software.

body.text: This mandatory CAFS disclosure of total R&D costs charged to expense pursuant to ASC 730 establishes the non-negotiable starting baseline—termed ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D (FS R&D)—for all subsequent tax reconciliations under the Directive.
Federal Tax Standards Under IRC Section 41, IRC Section 174, and IRC Section 174A

Federal tax compliance for corporate research activities operates across distinct statutory provisions of the Internal Revenue Code that interact differently with the ASC 730 book baseline. IRC Section 41 governs the Credit for Increasing Research Activities (Research Credit), which incentivizes incremental domestic investment in QREs—comprising in-house wages for qualified services, supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, rental or lease costs of computers, and the applicable statutory percentage of contract research expenses—paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business. To qualify under IRC Section 41, research activities must satisfy a stringent four-part statutory test demonstrating that the work is technological in nature, intended to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of a product or process, conducted through a process of experimentation, and directed toward a permitted functional purpose for a specific business component. Furthermore, IRC Section 41(c)(5) imposes a base-period consistency rule requiring taxpayers to consider whether the types of activities and associated costs included in the current credit year occurred in the base years, though IRS FAQ guidance clarifies that following the Directive in the credit year does not require a taxpayer to recompute its historical base years using the Directive template.

Simultaneously, IRC Section 174 and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) define Research or Experimental (R&E) expenditures as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Prior to the effective date of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) amendments, IRC Section 174 permitted taxpayers to deduct R&E expenditures immediately in the taxable year paid or incurred, paralleling the immediate expensing mandate of FASB ASC 730. Because the definitions of R&D under ASC 730 and R&E under IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 41 shared substantial conceptual similarities, the IRS determined that audited U.S. GAAP R&D expenses offered a reliable, albeit over-inclusive, starting proxy for computing QREs once non-qualifying items were mechanically removed.

However, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 (i.e., beginning in 2022) and before January 1, 2025, the TCJA amendments to IRC Section 174 eliminated immediate expensing and mandated that taxpayers capitalize Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over 5 years for domestic research or 15 years for foreign research. This statutory shift severed the historical timing alignment between financial accounting and federal tax accounting. While ASC 730 continued to mandate immediate expensing for financial reporting, TCJA IRC Section 174 enforced multi-year tax capitalization, creating a timing and scope divergence that forced corporate tax departments to manage three distinct compliance bases simultaneously.

Subsequently, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72), commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which added IRC Section 174A and amended IRC Section 174. Under IRC Section 174A(a), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, taxpayers are permitted to deduct domestic research and experimental expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred, or alternatively elect under IRC Section 174A(c) to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. However, mandatory capitalization and 15-year ratable amortization under amended IRC Section 174 remain strictly in force for foreign research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning in 2025 and thereafter. Furthermore, while eligible small business taxpayers (meeting the gross receipts test) were granted an election under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(1) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B. 393) to apply IRC Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, large corporate LB&I taxpayers must account for remaining unamortized domestic SRE amounts previously capitalized during the 2022–2024 TCJA window under the transition rules and automatic accounting method change procedures of OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2), Revenue Procedure 2025-23 (Sections 7.01, 7.02, and 7.03), Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32. In addition, if a taxpayer does not elect the reduced research credit under IRC Section 280C on Item A of Form 6765, it must reduce its domestic R&E expenditures under IRC Section 174A (whether deducted or capitalized) by the amount of the research credit.

Provides the audited starting baseline (ASC 730 FS R&D) reconciled to Schedule M-3.

Offers no legal determination, safe harbor, or computational shortcut; IRC §§ 174 and 174A bases must be computed separately.

body.text: Administrative Mechanics of the IRS ASC 730 Directive
Legal Nature of the Administrative Safe Harbor

Substantiating QREs under a traditional IRC Section 41 examination demands extensive administrative resources from both corporate taxpayers and IRS LB&I examiners due to the fact-intensive, technical nature of the four-part qualification test. The ASC 730 Directive mitigates this examination burden by prescribing a standardized, mechanical reconciliation that converts currently expensed R&D reported on the taxpayer's CAFS (ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D) into a tax-adjusted figure termed Adjusted ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D (ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D). This conversion is governed by the Certification Statement in Appendix A, the reconciliation framework in Appendix B, the line-item adjustments detailed in Appendices C and D, and the definitional standards set forth in Appendix E of the Directive.

When an eligible LB&I taxpayer satisfies all mechanical reconciliation steps, retains the mandatory general ledger and personnel documentation specified in Part IV (2017 Directive) / Part V (2020 Revised Directive), and executes a formal Certification Statement (Appendix A) signed under penalties of perjury by an individual authorized under IRC Section 6062, LB&I examiners accept the resulting ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D figure as sufficient administrative evidence of QREs for the credit year without challenging those amounts.

A foundational legal distinction underpins this mechanism: as explicitly stated in Part I of the Directive and the IRS LB&I Directive FAQs, the ASC 730 Directive is not an official pronouncement of law and does not determine, as a matter of law, whether the underlying research activities reported under ASC 730 constitute "qualified research activities" within the meaning of IRC Section 41 or IRC Section 174. Rather, the IRS exercises administrative discretion to accept the mechanically reconciled GAAP figure as an evidentiary safe harbor. By preserving statutory authority over technical qualification while waiving project-level substantiation up to the safe harbor ceiling, the Directive transforms the audit process from a subjective engineering inquiry into an objective accounting verification of general ledger (GL) account balance details (debit and credit transaction entries), trial balance reconciliations, Schedule M-3 tie-outs, organizational charts, and audited financial disclosures.
Mechanical Conversion from ASC 730 FS R&D to ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D

Because the financial accounting definition of R&D under FASB ASC 730 is broader in several respects than the statutory definition of QREs under IRC Section 41, the Directive mandates a five-step sequence of mechanical subtractions and wage adjustments across Appendix C (Lines 1 through 22) and Appendix D (Lines 1 through 7), applying the definitions in Appendix E, to strip out statutorily ineligible outlays. IRS examiners verify these mechanical adjustments line by line starting from the separately disclosed R&D figure on the CAFS:

items: Step 1 — Financial Statement R&D Base and Non-Consolidated Entity Subtractions (Appendix C, Lines 1–1b in the 2020 Revised Directive; Steps 1–2, Lines 1–3a in the 2017 Directive): The computation begins on Line 1 with the Financial Statement R&D amount reported on the taxpayer's CAFS (or Form 10-K / Notes to CAFS). On Line 1a (Line 2 in the 2017 Directive), the taxpayer must subtract all book/GAAP R&D amounts attributable to related foreign (non-U.S.) entities, such as Controlled Foreign Corporations, consolidated into the financial statements. On Line 1b of the 2020 Revised Directive, the taxpayer must also subtract R&D expenses of U.S. entities included in the financial statements that are excluded from the taxpayer's consolidated federal income tax return, yielding U.S. Financial Statement R&D reconciled to Schedule M-3 (Form 1120, Schedule M-3, Part III, Column (a), Line 35; or Form 1120S / Form 1065, Schedule M-3, Part III, Column (a), Line 29).

Step 2 — Subtraction of Non-ASC 730 Amounts Commingled in U.S. Financial Statement R&D (Appendix C, Lines 2–4 in the 2020 Revised Directive): Added in the 2020 Revised Directive (LB&I-04-0820-0016) to remove non-qualifying software and commercial engineering costs, Step 2 requires the taxpayer to remove any non-ASC 730 costs that were included in the financial statement R&D caption. Specifically, Line 3a removes non-ASC 730 software development costs (such as software developed exclusively for delivery via the Cloud/SaaS under non-ASC 730 rules), and Line 3b removes costs associated with activities typically excluded from R&D under ASC 730-10-55-2 (such as engineering services performed during early phases of commercial production involving routine, ongoing efforts to improve an existing product). Subtracting Step 2 from Step 1 yields U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D on Line 4.

Step 3 — Mandatory Statutory Subtractions from U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D (Appendix C, Lines 5–11a): Step 3 strips out specific categories of costs that fail IRC Section 174 or IRC Section 41 requirements or require non-mechanical contract review:

Line 5 (IRC Section 174 Exclusions): Subtracts all U.S. ASC 730 GL accounts for expenditures not allowed under IRC Section 174, including quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising or promotions, acquisition of another's patent, model, production, or process, research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects, research expenditures in excess of reasonable amounts, and expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land or depreciable property.

Line 6 (Non-Wage, Non-Supply, Non-Contract Research & Overhead Exclusions): Subtracts all U.S. ASC 730 GL accounts that are non-wage, non-supply, and non-contract research—specifically removing depreciation, amortization, shipping, travel, training, rent, overhead, general and administrative (G&A) expenses, and all other items not eligible for IRC Section 41 QREs.

Line 7 (Research Performed Pursuant to Contracts / Funded Research Exclusion): Subtracts all U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D costs incurred for all agreements or contracts pursuant to which the taxpayer performed ASC 730 research in order to comply with the terms of the agreements or contracts. Crucially, while IRC Section 41 excludes research to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or third-party arrangement in which the taxpayer does not retain substantial rights or bear financial risk, the Directive explicitly mandates that these costs must be subtracted in full on Line 7 regardless of whether incurred in connection with Funded Research, because determining contractual rights, risks, and funding issues requires a non-mechanical legal review of the underlying contracts.

Line 8 (Complete Subtraction of Non-Employee / External Contractor Costs): Mandates a complete subtraction of all U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D costs incurred for all persons other than the taxpayer's employees (i.e., external contractors and non-employees) who performed ASC 730 research on behalf of the taxpayer. Although IRC Section 41(b) generally permits taxpayers to include the applicable statutory percentage of eligible contract research expenses in QREs, the Directive requires the removal of all contract research costs from the starting book figure on Line 8 because verifying third-party contract research eligibility requires an in-depth, non-mechanical review of the contracts for potential funding, rights, and risk issues. Consequently, Column A of Appendix B reports N/A for contract research expenses; any qualified contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b) must be isolated, subjected to the applicable statutory percentage limitation, and claimed outside the safe harbor in Column B or Column C of Appendix B.

Line 9 (Foreign In-House R&D Costs): Requires the complete subtraction of all U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D in-house research performed outside the geographical boundaries of the United States, including wages, related expenses, and stock options for U.S. employees who leave the United States and perform research services outside the United States, in accordance with the domestic performance mandate of IRC Section 41.
Line 10 (Prototype Overhead, Patent Costs, and Severance Pay): Subtracts all prototype overhead expenses, patent costs, and severance pay included in U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D.
Lines 11 and 11a: Line 11 sums all Step 3 subtractions, and Line 11a yields the Subtotal U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D After Subtractions.

Step 4 — Employee Wage Replacement and Appendix D / Appendix E Wage Limitations (Appendix C, Lines 12–18 & Appendix D, Lines 1–7): Step 4 executes a multi-step replacement of book compensation with tax-eligible W-2 compensation. First, the taxpayer subtracts all remaining U.S. ASC 730 book wage and wage-related GL accounts not previously subtracted on Line 13 and subtracts all remaining book Stock-Based Compensation (SBC) on Line 14, leaving no book wages in the computation. Next, guided by the definitions in Appendix E and the schedule in Appendix D, the taxpayer adds back allowable taxable W-2 wages (comprising Base W-2 Wages defined under IRC Section 3401(a) excluding taxable stock options, plus W-2 Stock Options included in Form W-2 Box 1 wages) strictly for employees whose wage costs are charged to U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement Cost Centers (and excluding any W-2 wages attributable to book wages or stock options removed in Steps 1, 2, or 3):

Line 15 (Qualified Individual Contributors — 95% Rule): Adds back 95% of Base W-2 Wages (Appendix D, Line 1) and 95% of W-2 Stock Options (Appendix D, Line 2) for Qualified Individual Contributors (QICs)—defined in Appendix E as employees of the taxpayer who do not manage any taxpayer employees and whose wages are charged to U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement Cost Centers.

Line 16 (1st Level Supervisor Managers — 95% Rule): Adds back 95% of Base W-2 Wages (Appendix D, Line 4) and 95% of W-2 Stock Options (Appendix D, Line 5) for 1st Level Supervisor Managers—defined in Appendix E as managers that directly manage only Qualified Individual Contributors and whose wages are charged to U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement Cost Centers.

Line 17 (Upper Level Managers' Limit — 10% Cap): Adds the Upper Level Managers' Limit computed on Appendix D, Line 7. Appendix E defines Upper Level Managers (ULMs) as managers that directly supervise any employee other than Qualified Individual Contributors and whose wages are charged to U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement Cost Centers. Under Appendix D, Line 7, the allowable ULM wage addition is the lesser of: (a) 10% of the sum of total allowed QIC and 1st Level Supervisor Manager W-2 wages (the sum of Appendix D, Lines 3 and 6), or (b) 100% of the W-2 wage and W-2 stock option costs for Upper Level Managers charged to U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement Cost Centers. IRS FAQ guidance confirms that taxpayers are not required to claim either the 95% limitation or the 10% ULM limitation on Appendix D; however, if a taxpayer wants to include more than the 10% Upper Level Managers' Limit in QREs, 100% of the W-2 wage and W-2 stock option costs for Upper Level Managers on Appendix D is considered to be $0, and any qualifying ULM wages claimed under IRC Section 41 must be reported in Appendix B, Column B, where they are subject to IRS risk analysis and examination. Conversely, if the taxpayer claims the 10% limit per Appendix D, it may not claim any remaining excess ULM wages in Column B of Appendix B.

Step 5 — Final Adjusted ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D Allocation (Appendix C, Lines 19–22): Line 19 totals the final ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D safe harbor amount and disaggregates it across Line 20 (Wages for qualified services, corresponding to Form 6765 Line 5 or 24), Line 21 (Cost of supplies, Form 6765 Line 6 or 25), and Line 22 (Rental or lease costs of computers, Form 6765 Line 7 or 26), which are transferred directly into Column A of Appendix B.

cells: Foreign Entities & Non-Consolidated U.S. Entities
Step 1 (Lines 1a & 1b, 2020 Appendix C; Line 2, 2017 Appendix C)
Strips out R&D expenses of Controlled Foreign Corporations and non-consolidated domestic entities to tie CAFS R&D to the federal consolidated return and Schedule M-3.
Non-ASC 730 Software & Routine Engineering
Step 2 (Lines 3a & 3b, 2020 Appendix C)
Removes cloud/SaaS software development and routine commercial engineering excluded under ASC 730-10-55-2 that were commingled in book R&D.
Costs Outside Statutory R&E Scope (IRC § 174 Exclusions)
Step 3, Line 5, Appendix C
Strips out routine quality control testing, efficiency/management studies, consumer surveys, patent acquisitions, and land/depreciable property disallowed under IRC § 174.
Depreciation, Facilities & Indirect Overhead
Step 3, Line 6 & Line 10, Appendix C

Excludes non-wage, non-supply, non-contract GL accounts (depreciation, amortization, rent, utilities, travel, training, G&A overhead) and Line 10 prototype overhead, patent costs, and severance pay barred from IRC § 41 QREs.
Contract-Performed & Funded Research Expenditures
Step 3, Line 7, Appendix C
Removes all R&D costs incurred by the taxpayer to comply with contract terms—regardless of whether funded under IRC § 41—because evaluating contractual rights and risk is non-mechanical.
Non-Employee / External Contractor Costs
Step 3, Line 8, Appendix C

Subtracts all third-party non-employee research costs from the book baseline so that any qualified contract research is separately subjected to the applicable statutory percentage limitation under IRC § 41(b) in Appendix B, Columns B or C.
Foreign In-House R&D Costs
Step 3, Line 9, Appendix C
Eliminates salaries, supplies, stock options, and expenses for in-house research performed outside the United States (including U.S. employees working abroad) per IRC § 41.
Book-to-Tax Wage & Stock-Based Compensation Swap
Step 4 (Lines 13–17, Appendix C), Appendix D & Appendix E

Removes remaining book wages (Line 13) and book SBC (Line 14), replacing them with 95% of W-2 Base Wages and W-2 Stock Options for Qualified Individual Contributors (Line 15) and 1st Level Supervisor Managers (Line 16), plus the 10% Upper Level Managers' Limit (Line 17).

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Examples of the Directive Reconciliation
Hypothetical Scenario 1: Pharmaceutical Manufacturer Appendix C Reconciliation

Consider a hypothetical large pharmaceutical manufacturer that qualifies as an LB&I taxpayer (possessing assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000) and elects to compute its QREs pursuant to the ASC 730 Directive on its original timely filed return. On its Certified Audited Financial Statements (and reconciled to Schedule M-3, Part III, Line 35) for the taxable year, the corporation reports its total currently expensed U.S. ASC 730 R&D costs (ASC 730 FS R&D) on Appendix C, Line 4.
To arrive at ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D under Step 3 of Appendix C, the taxpayer executes three mandatory Appendix C subtractions:

items: First, under Line 7 of Appendix C, the company subtracts all funded/contract research costs resulting from a non-profit foundation grant received to execute a specific stage of clinical trials, as funded research is statutorily excluded under IRC Section 41 and all contract-compliance research must be removed on Line 7.

Second, under Line 9 of Appendix C, the company subtracts all foreign in-house research costs incurred for salaries and laboratory supplies at an overseas formulation laboratory, since QREs must be performed within the United States.

Third, under Line 8 of Appendix C, the company subtracts all amounts paid to external, non-employee contractors who performed research on the taxpayer's behalf, fulfilling the Directive's requirement to remove all non-employee research costs from the starting baseline.

body.text: The mechanical reconciliation follows the exact Appendix C arithmetic:

items: ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D (Appendix C, Line 19 / Appendix B, Column A) = Starting U.S. ASC 730 FS R&D (Line 4) − Funded/Contract Research Costs (Line 7) − Foreign In-House Research Costs (Line 9) − Non-Employee Contractor Research Costs (Line 8).

body.text: The resulting ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D figure is accepted by LB&I examiners as sufficient administrative evidence of QREs for the taxable year, shielding that base amount from a project-by-project technical audit.
Hypothetical Scenario 2: Enterprise Cost-Center Bridge with Stock-Based Compensation

In a second hypothetical model illustrating broader general ledger adjustments across Appendices B, C, and D, an LB&I enterprise begins with its Total GAAP R&D Expense reported on its CAFS (Appendix C, Line 1). From this baseline, the taxpayer subtracts its foreign research expenses conducted outside the United States (Appendix C, Line 1a / Line 9) and subtracts its non-qualifying depreciation and indirect overhead embedded within its R&D cost centers (Appendix C, Line 6).

Subsequently, in Step 4 of Appendix C (Lines 13–18) and Appendix D (Lines 1–7), after removing book wages (Line 13) and book stock-based compensation (Line 14), the taxpayer adds back qualified taxable W-2 Base Wages and W-2 Stock Options (95% for Qualified Individual Contributors on Line 15, 95% for 1st Level Supervisor Managers on Line 16, and the 10% Upper Level Managers' Limit on Line 17) attributable to eligible research personnel. Recomputing the reconciliation step by step yields the final safe harbor floor:

items: Final Safe Harbor QRE Floor (ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D, Appendix C, Line 19) = Total GAAP R&D Expense (Line 1) − Foreign Research Expenses (Lines 1a & 9) − Non-Qualifying Depreciation and Indirect Overhead (Line 6) + Net Qualified W-2 Wage & Stock-Based Compensation Adjustment (Step 4, Lines 13–18 / Appendix D).

body.text: Examination Scope, Audit Risk Floor, and Incremental Claims

The primary strategic benefit of complying with the ASC 730 Directive is the establishment of an audit-protected "floor" for the research credit claim. Provided the taxpayer satisfies all CAFS disclosure, Schedule M-3 tie-out, mechanical adjustment, documentation retention, and perjury certification requirements, LB&I examiners will not challenge QREs claimed up to the computed ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D figure reported in Column A of Appendix B. Furthermore, operational efficiency increases during quarterly financial statement tax provision cycles (Q1 through Q3) because corporate tax departments can estimate the credit directly from available GAAP R&D accounts rather than conducting retrospective employee time surveys.

However, the Directive enforces strict boundary limitations on incremental claims reported in Column B (additional QREs from ASC 730 accounts not included in ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D, such as qualifying contract research removed on Line 8, wage/supply/contract costs from customer agreements removed on Line 7, or excess Upper Level Manager wages omitted from Line 17) and Column C (additional QREs not from ASC 730 accounts, such as non-ASC 730 software development removed in Step 2) of Appendix B. Taxpayers frequently evaluate a hybrid filing strategy: locking in the ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D safe harbor floor in Column A for the primary portion of the claim while claiming an incremental slice of higher-risk additional QREs on Form 6765 via Columns B and C of Appendix B.

When a taxpayer claims QREs on Form 6765 that exceed the calculated ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D amount, Part II.C of the Directive and the IRS LB&I Practice Unit explicitly mandate that those incremental amounts fall outside the safe harbor and are immediately subjected to IRS risk assessment to determine the scope of an examination, including identification of the business components associated with the expenses, verification of all IRC Section 41 requirements, mandatory MITRE referrals if non-ASC 730 software development costs in Column C meet referral thresholds, and Uncertain Tax Position (UTP) evaluation. Moreover, if a taxpayer fails to separately identify ASC 730 R&D costs on its CAFS, fails to reconcile those CAFS to Schedule M-3, or fails to execute the mandatory mechanical adjustments, the taxpayer forfeits eligibility for the Directive's protection entirely.
Structural Conflicts in the Post-TCJA and Post-OBBBA Compliance Landscape
The Triple Reconciliation Dilemma Under IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 174A

While the ASC 730 Directive functioned smoothly when pre-TCJA IRC Section 174 allowed the immediate deduction of R&E outlays in parallel with U.S. GAAP, the post-2021 statutory evolution of IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 174A has introduced an arduous triple reconciliation burden. For taxable years beginning in 2022 through 2024 under TCJA Section 174—and continuing in 2025 and subsequent years for foreign R&E expenditures under amended IRC Section 174, elective domestic amortization under IRC Section 174A(c), and unamortized 2022–2024 TCJA capitalization pools under OBBBA Section 70302(f) and Revenue Procedures 2025-28 and 2026-32—corporate tax departments must simultaneously track and reconcile three distinct accounting and tax bases:

items: The FASB ASC 730 Book Expense Base: Immediately expensed on the Certified Audited Financial Statements and reconciled to Schedule M-3.
The IRC Section 41 QRE Credit Base: Derived via the Directive's mechanical subtractions in Appendix C and wage replacements in Appendix D (plus any non-Directive QREs in Appendix B, Columns B and C).

The IRC Section 174 / Section 174A Tax R&E Base: Capitalized and amortized over 5 years (domestic) and 15 years (foreign) for 2022–2024 under TCJA Section 174, and governed for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, by immediate domestic deduction (or elective ≥60-month amortization) under IRC Section 174A (reduced by the Section 280C credit adjustment unless the reduced credit is elected) alongside mandatory 15-year capitalization of foreign R&E under IRC Section 174.

body.text: This tripartite framework requires corporate tax teams to classify research expenditures across three distinct legal and accounting definitions, each governed by divergent inclusion and exclusion rules. Crucially, as confirmed in the IRS LB&I FAQs, the ASC 730 Directive provides administrative relief solely for substantiating QREs under IRC Section 41; it does not determine whether activities constitute qualified research under IRC Section 174 or Section 174A, and it provides no safe harbor, computational shortcut, or legal relief for determining R&E expenditures under IRC Section 174 or Section 174A.
Divergence Between Narrow ASC 730 Cost Centers and Broad IRC Section 174 Scope

A major source of compliance friction stems from the statutory and regulatory breadth of IRC Section 174 and Section 174A relative to FASB ASC 730 and the Directive's cost-center boundaries. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) and § 1.174-2(b)(1)—as further illustrated in IRS Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919) and Notice 2024-12 (2024-5 I.R.B. 616)—R&E and SRE expenditures encompass all costs "incident to" the development or improvement of a product or process, including the costs of obtaining a patent (such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application) and annual allowances for depreciation or depletion on property used in connection with research or experimentation.

For example, the allocation methodology in IRS Notice 2023-63 illustrates how broad "incident to" SRE expenditures must be captured across corporate departments: if a taxpayer incurs $200,000 in total facility depreciation, it must allocate that depreciation to SRE expenditures based on square footage and research time across its Research Department ($20,000, reflecting 1,000 of 10,000 square feet at 100% research time), Engineering Department ($4,000, reflecting 1,000 of 10,000 square feet at 20% research time), and Legal Department ($2,000, reflecting 1,000 of 10,000 square feet at 10% research time) for a facility depreciation SRE total of $26,000, alongside $150,000 (100% of $150,000) of depreciation on computers, furniture, and equipment used exclusively by the Research Department, $20,000 (20% of $100,000) of equipment depreciation from the Engineering Department, and $2,000 (10% of $20,000) of computer and furniture depreciation from the Legal Department, in addition to $50,000 of direct research materials and supplies. Similarly, depreciation with respect to a test bed used in SRE activities must be included under the "incident to" standard.

Conversely, the ASC 730 Directive captures only those costs directly recorded in U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D General Ledger accounts and disclosed in the R&D expense line item on the CAFS. Furthermore, even when depreciation, rent, utilities, patent legal costs, and overhead are recorded inside an ASC 730 R&D cost center for GAAP purposes, Step 3, Line 6 and Line 10 of Appendix C explicitly mandate that they be subtracted in full to compute ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D because they are barred from IRC Section 41 QREs. Similarly, depending on a corporation's internal GAAP cost accounting methodology, wages of research support personnel or software developers working on internal-use or cloud/SaaS platforms may be categorized in general operational accounts outside the disclosed ASC 730 R&D line item. When those costs are excluded from the CAFS R&D disclosure, IRS FAQ A7 confirms that they cannot be incorporated into the Directive's Column A baseline. Consequently, corporate taxpayers are forced into a demanding operational posture: they must either pursue excluded qualifying costs through high-friction traditional IRC Section 41 documentation in Column C of Appendix B, forgo those incremental credit amounts for simplicity, or maintain two parallel compliance systems—a top-down cost-center reconciliation for the IRC Section 41 credit under the Directive and a broader bottom-up cost-allocation architecture for IRC Section 174 and Section 174A.
Operational Contradictions and Administrative Resolution Under Revised IRS Form 6765 (Section E and Section G)

A second acute regulatory conflict arose from the IRS's implementation of a substantially revamped Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) (Rev. December 2024 and subsequent 2025/2026 instructions). The revised Form 6765 introduced Section E (Other Information), Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), and Section G (Business Component Information), the last of which requires taxpayers to disaggregate and report QREs categorized by specific "business components" across Columns 49(a) through 56.

In its initial conception, a rigid component-by-component reporting mandate directly conflicted with the administrative efficiency that forms the core purpose of the ASC 730 Directive. The Directive was expressly engineered to streamline audits by accepting a single, consolidated aggregate figure (ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D) derived from the taxpayer's certified books and general ledger cost centers, thereby sidestepping the burden of linking every expenditure back to specific business-component research testing under IRC Section 41. Because a taxpayer complying with the Directive computes a single consolidated QRE total from trial balance cost centers on Appendix C, the taxpayer does not generate disaggregated business-component figures in the course of preparing Appendices A through D.
Addressing this tension, the IRS incorporated specific operational rules for ASC 730 Directive filers into the official Instructions for Form 6765 (updated through February 6, 2026):

items: Phased Effective Date for Section G: The Instructions for Form 6765 state that for taxable years beginning before 2026, Section G is optional for all filers on original returns. For taxable years beginning after 2025, Section G is required, subject to exemptions for (a) a qualified small business under IRC Section 41(h)(3) that checks the box to claim a reduced payroll tax credit (up to the $500,000 annual limit), or (b) a filer whose total QREs determined at the controlled group level on Line 48 are equal to or less than $1.5 million, whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are equal to or less than $50 million, and that is reporting a research credit on an original return.

Mandatory Section E, Line 41 Election and Standardized E-File Attachments: If a taxpayer is eligible and chooses to follow the ASC 730 Directive, it must check "Yes" on Line 41 of Section E. When e-filing, the taxpayer must attach ASC 730 Directive Appendices A, B, C, and D using four exact PDF file naming conventions: Form6765ASC730AppendixA.pdf, Form6765ASC730AppendixB.pdf, Form6765ASC730AppendixC.pdf, and Form6765ASC730AppendixD.pdf.

The "ASC 730 Directive Single Entry for Section G" Rule: For the amount reported on Line 41, the Form 6765 Instructions permit the taxpayer to enter "ASC 730 Directive" on a single row in Column 49(c) of Section G, and enter the applicable wage, supply, and computer rental amounts from ASC 730 Directive Appendix B (Column A only) into Columns 53, 54, 55, and 56 (the total of which must equal Line 41), with no other columns in Section G required for that single entry.

The 80% / Top 50 Threshold and Residual Conflict for Hybrid Filers: Taxpayers required to complete Section G must generally report by business component (in descending order of total QREs) a minimum of 80% of total QREs (on Line 48) or a maximum of 50 business components, reporting any remaining components on a single row labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c). Under the Form 6765 Instructions, if the "ASC 730 Directive" single entry (Appendix B, Column A) accounts for at least 80% of total QREs reported on Line 48, no additional business components need to be reported. However, if an LB&I taxpayer claims non-Directive QREs in Columns B and C of Appendix B (such as qualified contract research expenses removed on Appendix C Line 8, or non-ASC 730 cloud/internal-use software costs removed on Line 3a) that exceed 20% of total Line 48 QREs, the "ASC 730 Directive" single entry accounts for less than 80% of total QREs. In that case, the instructions mandate that additional business components must be reported in Section G (completing Columns 49(a)–(f) and 50–56) to meet the 80% / Top 50 business component requirement. Consequently, for LB&I taxpayers with substantial third-party contract research or non-ASC 730 software development exceeding 20% of total QREs, Section G continues to impose a major project-level compliance burden.

body.text: Tactical Implementation and Regulatory Recommendations
Corporate Implementation Protocol for LB&I Taxpayers
For eligible LB&I corporations moving from theoretical evaluation to tactical implementation of the ASC 730 Directive, execution follows a three-stage operational protocol:

items: Stage 1 — Comprehensive Gap Analysis, 80% Section G Threshold Modeling, and Feasibility Study: First, the corporate tax department must perform a comprehensive gap analysis and feasibility study comparing its traditional QRE calculation methodology against the ADJ ASC 730 FS R&D safe harbor result in Appendix B, Column A. Because the Directive excludes expenses outside the CAFS R&D line item, applies a 95% inclusion rate to QIC and 1st Level Supervisor Manager W-2 wages, caps Upper Level Manager wages at 10%, and requires a complete baseline subtraction of contract-performed research (Line 7) and non-employee contractor costs (Line 8) prior to statutory adjustments in Columns B and C, tax leadership must evaluate whether the resulting reduction ("haircut") in Column A QREs is justified by the audit certainty of the safe harbor floor. Furthermore, for tax years beginning after 2025, tax teams must evaluate whether the Appendix B, Column A amount equals at least 80% of total Line 48 QREs on Form 6765 to preserve the "ASC 730 Directive" single-entry exemption in Section G.

Stage 2 — General Ledger (GL) Mapping Review and Organizational Chart Alignment: Second, corporate accounting and tax teams must execute a thorough General Ledger mapping review, tying the CAFS R&D disclosure to Schedule M-3 (Part I, Line 4(b) and Part III, Line 35), extracting transaction-level account balance details (debit and credit entries) for all ASC 730 R&D GL accounts, mapping trial balance accounts directly to the specific adjustment lines on Appendix C (Steps 1 through 5), distinguishing purely ASC 730 R&D cost centers from mixed-activity or non-ASC 730 cost centers, and aligning Human Resources organizational charts and reporting levels to classify employees into Qualified Individual Contributors, 1st Level Supervisor Managers, and Upper Level Managers on Appendix D.

Stage 3 — Perjury Certification, E-File Attachment Compliance, and IDR Readiness Package: Third, the taxpayer must prepare and execute the mandatory Appendix A Certification Statement signed under penalties of perjury by an individual authorized under IRC Section 6062, check "Yes" on Line 41 of Form 6765 Section E, and attach Form6765ASC730AppendixA.pdf through Form6765ASC730AppendixD.pdf when e-filing its original timely filed return. Simultaneously, the tax department must compile the mandatory Part IV / Part V examination documentation package—comprising all Step 1–4 GL account balance details, organizational charts, executed contracts for Line 7 and Line 8 research, and the Step 4 employee W-2 roster identifying job titles, reporting levels, and cost centers—for timely submission upon receipt of an LB&I Information Document Request (IDR).

body.text: Recommended Administrative and Policy Clarifications

Analysis of the structural tensions between the ASC 730 Directive, the post-TCJA and post-OBBBA IRC Section 174 / Section 174A regimes, and the revised Form 6765 demonstrates that targeted administrative action by the Department of the Treasury and the IRS is warranted to preserve and strengthen the Directive's operational viability:

items: Expansion of Form 6765 Section G Single-Entry Relief to Audited ASC 730 Contract Research in Appendix B, Column B: While the IRS's creation of the "ASC 730 Directive Single Entry for Section G" in the 2025/2026 Form 6765 Instructions addressed the Section G reporting conflict for taxpayers whose Appendix B, Column A safe harbor accounts for at least 80% of total QREs, LB&I taxpayers that incur substantial third-party contract research expenses recorded within their audited ASC 730 GL accounts must still subtract 100% of those contractor costs on Appendix C, Line 8 and claim the applicable statutory percentage in Appendix B, Column B. If those Column B contract research QREs push non-Column A QREs above 20% of Line 48 total QREs, the taxpayer loses the single-entry shield and must disaggregate business components in Section G. The IRS should issue supplemental Form 6765 guidance permitting taxpayers to include or aggregate audited ASC 730 contract research reported in Appendix B, Column B within simplified Section G reporting.

Integrated Reconciliation Guidance Bridging ASC 730, IRC Section 174, and IRC Section 174A: Building upon Notice 2023-63, Notice 2024-12, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32, the Treasury Department and the IRS should publish a comprehensive Revenue Procedure or Technical Advice Memorandum establishing clear reconciliation rules for indirect costs—such as allocated overhead, facility rent, utilities, and depreciation on R&D assets subtracted on Appendix C, Line 6—that are captured within the broad "incident to" base of IRC Section 174 and Section 174A but excluded from the narrower ASC 730 FS R&D baseline and IRC Section 41 QREs, demonstrating how a single set of research activities reconciles across all three compliance bases.

Policy Review to Scale the Directive Concept to Non-LB&I Entities: The IRS should conduct a policy review to evaluate expanding the scope of the Directive concept to non-LB&I entities (assets under $10,000,000). While the Directive is currently restricted strictly to LB&I taxpayers with Certified Audited Financial Statements, conditional administrative relief could potentially be scaled to smaller innovative entities that prepare audited or reviewed U.S. GAAP financial statements or claim the research credit under the IRC Section 41(h) payroll tax offset provisions, thereby lowering compliance barriers to domestic innovation.

Modernization of LB&I Practice Units and Examiner Training Materials: Finally, LB&I Practice Unit DCN COR-P-032 (Revised ASC 730 Directive - Computing Qualified Research Expenses, last updated April 22, 2021) and examiner training materials should be updated alongside IRM 4.30.2.11.4 to reflect the post-TCJA and post-OBBBA regulatory environment, including IRC Section 174A and the revised Form 6765 Section E and Section G procedures. Updated training should explicitly contrast ASC 730 book costs, IRC Section 41 QREs, IRC Section 174A domestic R&E expenditures, and IRC Section 174 foreign R&E expenditures, reinforcing for both examiners and corporate tax professionals that the ASC 730 Directive provides administrative relief strictly for IRC Section 41 credit substantiation and does not alter a taxpayer's statutory obligations under IRC Section 174 or Section 174A.
